content.text:
This Annual Review covered Year 1 delivery under FCDO programme code MWI-EDU-AR-4471. The award letter defined the first Annual Review period as 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025, although partner returns used 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 and finance had not yet recut to the FCDO review window. The programme remained broadly on track against its Year 1 plan and continued to contribute to the intended outcome that girls demonstrate improved retention, attendance and learning continuity.

Results were mixed but positive overall. Re-enrolment and retention exceeded plan: OP1.1 reached 684 girls against a Year 1 target of 650. Remedial learning also exceeded target, with 438 girls completing at least 20 sessions against a target of 420. Attendance at 80% or more reached 472 girls against a target of 500, below milestone because four schools submitted attendance registers late. Under the safer school environment output, rehabilitation of separate lockable girls' latrine stances exceeded target, with 31 completed against a target of 24. However, schools with menstrual health supplies and trained focal teachers reached 17 against a target of 20; records attributed this shortfall to menstrual health supply delays, and three schools lacked a female focal teacher for training.

Household support largely met planned levels. Education hardship grants reached 392 caregivers against a target of 400, while school re-entry kits or learning materials reached 571 girls against a target of 550. Follow-up verification within 45 days for hardship grant households reached 0.68 against a target of 0.75, so case management did not keep pace with grant delivery in all cases during the review period. System strengthening outputs were also close to plan: district learning meetings reached 3 against a target of 4, while training on girls' re-entry and safeguarding protocols exceeded plan at 136 school and community actors against a target of 120.

Evidence for reported results came from school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists, and district validation samples. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, and monitoring relied on termly indicator returns and partner spot checks rather than a standalone external evaluation in Year 1. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, with no major incident trend reported in Year 1 monitoring returns. No new material risks were reported beyond those already captured in the grant risk register. There was also no evidence that funds were used other than as intended; hardship grant checks deduplicated 16 caregiver records before payment.

Financial delivery ran slightly above forecast across sampled output lines in the AR1 export: actual spend totalled GBP 694,860 against forecast GBP 653,000. Variance appears linked in part to higher lake-shore transport costs under OP1.1 and stronger-than-planned delivery on several outputs.

Agreed follow-up actions were clear. The Programme Manager was to recut AR1 reporting to the FCDO review window by Q1 of the next period; M&E was to secure missing Term 3 registers from four schools; and WASH was to close the remaining OP2.2 gap, including completion of disposal bins at four latrine units and menstrual health training in the three remaining schools.

content.text:
The programme’s stated outcome was that girls demonstrate improved retention, attendance and learning continuity. During the review period, outcome monitoring used term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks. Reported results showed improvement against Year 1 milestones, with stronger performance on retention and mixed performance on attendance and selected enabling outputs.

Progress against expected results was broadly on track. Under Output 1, 684 girls were re-enrolled or retained against a Year 1 target of 650. Attendance at 80% or more of school days reached 472 against a target of 500, while 438 girls completed at least 20 remedial learning sessions against a target of 420. This pattern suggested that re-entry and remedial support were delivered at or above plan, but regular attendance lagged behind target.

Under Output 2, delivery on safer and more supportive school conditions was mixed. The programme rehabilitated 31 separate lockable girls’ latrine stances against a target of 24. By contrast, 17 schools had menstrual health supplies and trained focal teachers against a target of 20. The reported shortfall was linked to menstrual health supply delays. A related assumption held in most schools, but three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training.

Under Output 3, direct support to households and girls largely tracked close to plan. The programme reached 392 caregivers with an education hardship grant against a target of 400, and 571 girls received a school re-entry kit or learning materials against a target of 550. However, verified attendance follow-up within 45 days reached 0.68 against a target of 0.75, showing weaker case follow-up than planned.

Under Output 4, district and community systems also showed mixed progress. Three district learning meetings were held with documented action points against a target of four, while 136 school or community actors were trained on girls re-entry and safeguarding protocols against a target of 120. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and Year 1 monitoring returns did not report any major incident trend.

Taken together, these results supported the conclusion that delivery contributed to the outcome objective, especially through stronger re-enrolment or retention performance, remedial participation, school infrastructure rehabilitation, material support to girls, and training of school and community actors. The main areas where performance fell below milestone were attendance at the expected threshold, menstrual health coverage in schools, verified follow-up after hardship grants, and the number of district learning meetings completed.

The main deviations were explained in the available evidence. Four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting. Menstrual health supply delays reduced OP2.2 delivery to 17 of the planned 20 schools. No new material risks beyond those already recorded in the grant risk register were reported, although lake-shore transport costs increased for OP1.1. No major climate shock stopped delivery in Year 1.

Evidence for this assessment was adequate for routine annual review purposes but had limits. Indicator actuals were drawn from the BridgeLight AR1 export with source notes per output, and evidence included school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists, and district validation samples. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures. No standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year 1; monitoring relied on termly indicator returns and partner spot checks.

There were also data quality issues that affect interpretation. Partner returns used a review period of 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 while the award letter cited 15-Oct-2024 to 14-Oct-2025 for the first Annual Review period; finance had not recut the period at the time of reporting. This means trend interpretation should be read as broadly indicative of Year 1 performance rather than as a fully aligned review window.

Overall, performance was credible and mostly positive for Year 1. Delivery exceeded several annual milestones and remained close to plan on others, but weaker attendance reporting and incomplete menstrual health coverage limited progress toward the full outcome standard during the period.

Evidence was taken from school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists and district validation samples.

content.text:
Monitoring during the review period relied on routine programme records rather than a standalone evaluation. Indicator actuals were drawn from the BridgeLight AR1 export, with source notes recorded per output, and the evidence base included school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists, and district validation samples. Monitoring also relied on termly indicator returns and partner spot checks. This provided a usable basis for reviewing delivery against the logframe, and submitted records supported assessment of both results and spending at output level.

The evidence was strongest where administrative records could be checked against more than one source. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, and financial lines in the AR1 export included budget-to-actual comparisons. Submitted records therefore gave reasonable assurance for several Year 1 output claims, including OP1.1 at 684 against a target of 650, OP2.1 at 31 against a target of 24, and OP4.3 at 136 against a target of 120. They also showed areas where performance was below milestone: OP1.2 reached 472 against a target of 500, OP2.2 reached 17 against a target of 20, OP3.1 reached 392 against a target of 400, OP3.3 reached 0.68 against a target of 0.75, and OP4.1 reached 3 against a target of 4.

Evidence quality was weaker for attendance-related reporting than for re-entry or infrastructure outputs. Four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting. The records still indicated that supported girls' attendance and retention improved against Year 1 milestones, using term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks, but this part of the assessment carried more uncertainty than indicators supported by complete administrative records.

There was also an unresolved reporting-period issue in the submitted evidence pack. Partner returns used 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25, while the award letter cited an Annual Review window from 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025; finance had not recut the period at the time of reporting. That mismatch did not invalidate the Year 1 results set, but it limited strict comparability with the FCDO review window and should be taken into account when reading both performance and expenditure figures.

No standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year 1. As a result, this section draws conclusions from monitoring evidence rather than from an independent effectiveness study. Within that limitation, the submitted records were sufficient to support a cautious assessment that delivery remained broadly on track overall, with clear shortfalls concentrated in attendance reporting follow-up and menstrual health supply coverage.
assumptions: No baseline or methodological rating scale for evidence quality was provided in submitted records, so evidence quality has been described narratively rather than scored.
The section refers to Year 1 output indicators recorded in the AR1 export because no separate evidence dataset for the stated report period of 2025-04-01 to 2026-03-31 was supplied.
Exact gender, age, or vulnerability disaggregation was not available in submitted records for this section despite the reporting obligation on disaggregated monitoring data.

content.text:
During the period, no new material risks were reported beyond those already captured in the grant risk register. The main delivery issue that materialised affected OP2.2: menstrual health supply delays contributed to performance of 17 schools reached against a target of 20. This shortfall aligned with a related assumption that focal teachers would be available in supported schools. That assumption held in most schools, but three schools did not have a female focal teacher available for menstrual health training during the period. These factors help explain why OP2.2 lagged while other output areas remained broadly on track.

Climate and operating conditions did not stop implementation in Year 1, although they did affect cost pressure. Lake-shore transport costs increased for OP1.1, and this sat alongside actual spend of GBP 174,850 against a budget of GBP 162,000 for that line. Even with that pressure, OP1.1 still exceeded its Year 1 target, reaching 684 girls re-enrolled or retained against a target of 650. This suggests that mitigation measures maintained delivery despite higher operating costs.

Financial control findings during the period were stable. Monitoring and payment controls found no evidence that funds were used other than as intended. For hardship grants, the programme deduplicated 16 caregiver records before payment, which reduced the risk of duplicate disbursement and showed that pre-payment checks were functioning. More broadly, Year 1 actual spend across sampled output lines totalled GBP 694,860 against forecast spend of GBP 653,000 in the AR1 export, so cost control will need continued attention alongside delivery performance.

Safeguarding controls remained active during the reporting period. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and Year 1 monitoring returns did not report any major incident trend. Training and system-strengthening activity also progressed: 136 school and community actors were trained on girls' re-entry and safeguarding protocols against a target of 120, and district learning meetings reached 3 against a target of 4 with documented action points. These measures supported oversight and case handling, even though exact incident disaggregation was not available in the submitted records.

The section's main control issues were therefore operational rather than systemic: delayed menstrual health inputs, uneven availability of female focal teachers in three schools, higher transport costs linked to lake-shore delivery routes, and routine data quality pressures already noted elsewhere in the review process. Overall, controls remained in place and were used: referral pathways were tested, payment lists were cleaned before transfer, and district validation samples confirmed key re-entry figures.

Named risk owners and status labels for table rows were not available in the submitted records.
Exact safeguarding incident counts or disaggregation were not available; narrative therefore reports only that no major incident trend was reported.

content.text:
Value for Money was assessed against economy, efficiency, effectiveness and equity using the AR1 export and confirmed monitoring notes. Year 1 actual spend on sampled output lines totalled GBP 694,860 against a forecast of GBP 653,000, so delivery ran above forecast overall. The main cost pressure noted in submitted records was increased lake-shore transport costs affecting OP1.1. At the same time, there was no evidence that funds were used other than intended, and hardship grant controls removed duplicate risk by deduplicating 16 caregiver records before payment.

On economy, the programme showed mixed performance. Some lines underspent against budget, including OP1.3 at GBP 81,330 against GBP 88,000, OP2.2 at GBP 39,600 against GBP 42,000, OP3.3 at GBP 24,980 against GBP 31,000 and OP4.1 at GBP 32,700 against GBP 39,000. Other lines overspent: OP1.1 reached GBP 174,850 against GBP 162,000; OP1.2 reached GBP 98,740 against GBP 94,000; OP2.1 reached GBP 148,900 against GBP 121,000; OP3.1 reached GBP 151,440 against GBP 146,000; OP3.2 reached GBP 109,250 against GBP 103,000; and OP4.3 reached GBP 58,630 against GBP 54,000. The largest variance sat on OP2.1. That overspend accompanied delivery above target, with 31 latrine stances rehabilitated against a target of 24. This suggests higher unit cost than planned but stronger physical delivery during the period.

On efficiency, several outputs converted spending into results at or above milestone level. OP1.1 achieved 684 girls re-enrolled or retained against a target of 650 despite transport cost pressure and after register cleaning reduced double-count risk. OP1.3 achieved 438 girls completing at least 20 remedial learning sessions against a target of 420 while spending below budget. OP3.2 reached 571 girls receiving school re-entry kits or learning materials against a target of 550 with moderate overspend relative to budget. OP4.3 trained 136 school or community actors against a target of 120.

Efficiency was weaker where delivery bottlenecks slowed conversion of inputs into results. OP1.2 reached 472 girls attending at least 80% of school days against a target of 500; four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected reporting completeness for this indicator. OP2.2 reached only 17 schools against a target of 20 because menstrual health supply delays affected implementation and three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. OP3.3 also fell short: verified attendance follow-up within 45 days reached a proportion of 0.68 against a target of 0.75.

On effectiveness, Year 1 delivery remained broadly on track and outcome monitoring reported improved attendance and retention for supported girls against Year 1 milestones. Results were strongest on re-entry support and school environment improvements: re-enrolment or retention exceeded target by reaching 684 girls; remedial learning exceeded target at 438 girls; latrine rehabilitation exceeded target at 31 stances; re-entry kits or learning materials exceeded target at reaching an additional group above the Year 1 milestone; and training on girls' re-entry and safeguarding protocols also surpassed plan at 136 participants compared with the target of120 . These gains supported the programme outcome that girls demonstrated improved retention, attendance and learning continuity.

Effectiveness was moderated by shortfalls in attendance consistency and menstrual health support coverage. Attendance at the eighty per cent threshold remained below plan, district learning meetings reached three against a target of four, and hardship grant follow-up did not meet the expected verification rate within forty-five days. No new material risks beyond those in the grant risk register were reported during the period, no major climate shock stopped delivery in Year
0Year
01 monitoring returns recorded no major incident trend.

On equity, available evidence showed that support channels were directed toward barriers that commonly affect girls' participation: hardship grants to caregivers reached392 households against a target of400; school re-entry kits or learning materials reached571 girls against a target of550; separate lockable girls' latrine stances were rehabilitated; menstrual health supplies and trained focal teachers were in place in17 schools; and safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools with no major incident trend reported in Year
01 monitoring returns. However, submitted records did not provide quantified disaggregation by age or vulnerability for this section even though disaggregated monitoring data was an FCDO reporting requirement.

Overall, Value for Money was acceptable but uneven across outputs in Year
01. The programme generated strong output delivery on several lines despite moderate overspend overall on sampled outputs and specific cost pressure on transport and WASH works. The clearest improvements needed were to align finance reporting to the FCDO review window of15 October2024 to14 October2025, close the remaining gap on OP2.2 by completing menstrual health training in the three remaining schools and finishing disposal bins at four latrine units, and secure late attendance registers so that efficiency and effectiveness judgements rest on complete evidence.
assumptions: No baseline or business case unit-cost benchmark was available in submitted records for direct comparison of planned versus actual cost per beneficiary or per output.

Equity assessment relied on proxy evidence from hardship grants, re-entry kits, menstrual health support and safeguarding measures because quantified age or vulnerability disaggregation was not available in submitted records for this section.
The statement on overall sampled output spend used the confirmed gap answer because no single consolidated total line was provided as a fact key.
Reporting-period alignment remained uncertain because partner returns used 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 while the award letter cited 15-Oct-24 to14-Oct-25; finance had not recut during the review period.

sections.label: F. Programme Management: Delivery, Commercial and Financial Performance

content.text:
Delivery in Year 1 remained broadly on track, with stronger performance on several output lines and some reporting and implementation issues that need follow-up. Re-entry and retention delivery exceeded plan: OP1.1 reached 684 girls against a Year 1 target of 650. Remedial learning also exceeded target, with 438 girls completing at least 20 sessions against a target of 420. School re-entry kits or learning materials reached 571 girls against a target of 550, and training on girls' re-entry and safeguarding protocols reached 136 school and community actors against a target of 120. WASH infrastructure delivery was ahead of plan on latrine rehabilitation, with 31 separate lockable girls' latrine stances completed against a target of 24.

Performance was weaker on a smaller set of indicators. Attendance at 80% or more reached 472 girls against a target of 500. Partner reporting confirmed that late attendance registers from four schools affected OP1.2 reporting. Menstrual health support reached 17 schools against a target of 20. Submitted risk information stated that menstrual health supply delays affected this result, and that three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. Hardship grant delivery was close to plan at 392 caregivers against a target of 400, but verified attendance follow-up within 45 days reached 0.68 against a target of 0.75. District learning meetings also fell slightly short, with three meetings held against a target of four.

Partner performance was mixed but acceptable overall. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, which supported confidence in OP1.1 results. At the same time, late register submission from four schools reduced the completeness of attendance reporting. Previous actions on register cleaning were only partly complete, although September deduplication removed double-count risk on OP1.1 and hardship grant checks removed duplicated caregiver records before payment.

Financial delivery ran above forecast across the sampled output lines in the AR1 export. Actual spend totalled GBP 694,860 against forecast spend of GBP 653,000. Overspends were recorded on several lines linked to outputs that met or exceeded targets, including OP1.1 at GBP 174,850 against GBP 162,000, OP2.1 at GBP 148,900 against GBP 121,000, OP3.1 at GBP 151,440 against GBP 146,000, OP3.2 at GBP 109,250 against GBP 103,000, and OP4.3 at GBP 58,630 against GBP 54,000. Some lines underspent: OP1.3 spent GBP 81,330 against GBP 88,000; OP2.2 spent GBP 39,600 against GBP 42,000; OP3.3 spent GBP 24,980 against GBP 31,000; and OP4.1 spent GBP 32,700 against GBP 39,000.

The available evidence suggests that overspend did not reflect weak control alone; in several cases it sat alongside over-delivery on outputs. However, one financial management issue remained unresolved in the review period: partner returns used a review window of 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 while the award letter set the first Annual Review period as 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025. Finance had not yet recut to the FCDO review window at the point of reporting, so comparability between delivery and financial reporting periods was not fully aligned.

No evidence suggested funds were used other than as intended. Hardship grant controls included deduplication of caregiver records before payment, and submitted information reported no new material risks beyond those already captured in the grant risk register. Commercial performance could only be assessed in limited terms from the submitted record: no supplier or consultant performance issues were reported in the evidence provided for this section.

On management actions and compliance with FCDO processes, the programme maintained documented district learning meetings and prepared for the review pack due under the award letter requirements. Follow-up actions were clearly identified: recut finance to the FCDO review window; chase late Term 3 attendance registers from four schools; complete menstrual health training in the three remaining schools; and finish disposal bins linked to four latrine units.
assumptions: No supplier or consultant names or contract-level performance data were available in submitted records; commercial performance is therefore reported only as 'no issues reported' based on available evidence.
The statement that actual spend totalled GBP 694,860 against forecast GBP 653,000 is taken from the human-confirmed gap answer covering sampled output lines in the AR1 export.

Because partner returns used a different review window from the award letter period and finance had not been recut, exact like-for-like comparison across all delivery and finance data remained limited.

content.text:
Recommendations from the current review focused on three corrective actions. First, the team identified the need to recut finance to the FCDO review window of 15 October to 14 October, as partner returns were still using 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 and finance had not yet been recut. Second, the review highlighted the need to complete menstrual health training in the three remaining schools, linked to OP2.2 performance of 17 schools reached against a target of 20. Third, the review called for submission of late attendance registers, as four schools submitted registers late and this affected OP1.2 reporting.

Updates on previous recommendations showed partial progress. Earlier actions on register cleaning were partly completed, and September deduplication removed double-count risk on OP1.1. This was consistent with district validation samples that confirmed re-entry figures, while attendance reporting remained weaker because of late submissions from four schools.

Priorities for the next period were therefore clear and evidence-based. The programme needed to close the OP2.2 gap from 17 of 20 schools, complete disposal bins at four latrine units, and align reporting period labelling with the award letter. These actions responded directly to Year 1 delivery issues rather than new material risks: no new material risks were reported beyond those already in the grant risk register.
